DEFERRED COMPENSATION AND EQUITY VESTING AT TERMINATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS EQUITY VESTING AT TERMINATION INFORMATION SHEET
This Deferred Compensation and Equity Vesting at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., which ended on October 1, 2026. It addresses a different legal question from the one covered by this project's Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document: not whether already-accrued vacation or paid time off must be paid out at termination, but how stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), and other equity compensation granted by Acme, Inc. are treated when employment ends — including whether unvested equity is itself a form of "wages" under California law, what governs whether unvested equity is forfeited when employment ends, and the separate federal tax mechanics that bear on how long a former employee has to exercise a vested-but-unexercised incentive stock option. The equity compensation addressed in this document is described as: incentive stock options, granted under: 2020 Equity Incentive Plan.

WHETHER UNVESTED EQUITY COMPENSATION IS "WAGES": AN UNRESOLVED STATUTORY TEXT
California's core wage statute defines "wages" broadly, as "all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description," measured by the standard of time, task, piece, "commission basis," or "other method of calculation." This definition expressly names commission-based pay as one of its examples, and California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement has separately published guidance treating a promised bonus tied to a specific result as falling within it as well. Stock options, restricted stock units, and other forms of equity compensation are not named anywhere in this statutory text, and no comparable published agency interpretation naming them was located this session. Whether, and under what circumstances, unvested equity compensation is or is not a "wage" within this definition is therefore a question this statute's own text does not resolve on its face.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of "wages" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence only of what Labor Code section 200(a)'s definition of "wages" does and does not name on its face — not a claim that unvested equity compensation is, or is not, a "wage" under California law, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 200(a)); the same subsection is already independently verified elsewhere in this project's own corpus, applied to commissions and to bonus pay respectively (this project's Commission Payout Upon Termination and Bonus and Incentive Compensation at Termination documents), and this clause does not treat those prior verifications as an independent second source — it instead fetched the same statutory text fresh, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, twice this session with two different User-Agent headers, and found it byte-identical both times. This clause separately confirmed, by fetching the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own published glossary pages for the letters E, S, and V directly from dir.ca.gov (each fetched and byte-compared across two User-Agent headers), that the glossary contains no entry for "equity," "stock option," "RSU," "restricted stock," or "vesting," as it does for "bonus." A California Supreme Court decision is widely reported, in secondary legal sources, to have addressed a closely related question — whether unvested, contingent equity-type compensation that is forfeited under a deferred-compensation plan's own terms when an employee voluntarily resigns is "wages already earned" that other Labor Code wage-protection statutes would prohibit an employer from taking back — commonly cited as Schachter v. Citigroup, Inc., 47 Cal. 4th 610 (2009). That decision was not independently fetched or read this session: CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit, confirmed exhausted this session with several hours remaining before reset) before it could be retrieved. No quotation from, or citation entry for, that decision is included in this clause's citations array as a result; it is described here only as a widely-reported case name and general subject matter, not as a verified holding, consistent with this tool's practice of not fabricating case-law quotations. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific stock option, RSU, or other equity award described in this document is or is not a "wage" under California law.

DISTINGUISHING EQUITY COMPENSATION FROM VACATION WAGES UNDER SECTION 227.3 AND SUASTEZ
California's vacation-vesting rule, addressed in full in this project's Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document, is built on a specific statute and a specific line of case law, neither of which mentions stock options, restricted stock units, or other equity compensation. Labor Code section 227.3's no-forfeiture protection applies, by its own text, only "whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations" — its operative language is limited to vacation, not to compensation generally. The California Supreme Court's reasoning in Suastez v. Plastic Dress-Up Co. for why vacation pay vests as it is earned rests on vacation's specific character as "deferred wages for services rendered" that vests "as the labor is rendered" — a day-by-day accrual tied to time already worked, rather than to a future date, cliff, or milestone that has not yet occurred. Because neither the statute's text nor this reasoning refers to equity compensation, this vacation-specific, no-forfeiture rule does not, by its own terms, extend to stock options, RSUs, or other equity awards, and no comparable California statute barring forfeiture of unvested equity compensation upon termination was located this session. Absent such a statute, whether and on what terms unvested equity is forfeited when employment with Acme, Inc. ends is instead governed by the terms of the specific equity plan, option agreement, or grant agreement under which the equity described in this document was awarded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=227.3.)
  "The right to a paid vacation, when offered in an employer's policy or contract of employment, constitutes deferred wages for services rendered. Case law from this state and others, as well as principles of equity and justice, compel the conclusion that a proportionate right to a paid vacation "vests" as the labor is rendered."
  — Suastez v. Plastic Dress-Up Co., 31 Cal. 3d 774 (1982) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1173656/suastez-v-plastic-dress-up-co/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence that section 227.3's anti-forfeiture protection and the Suastez vesting rationale are textually and doctrinally specific to vacation pay — not a claim that equity compensation could never be treated as earned or vested wages under some other legal theory, which this clause does not resolve. This session's CourtListener access was confirmed exhausted (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit) before the Suastez opinion could be independently re-fetched and re-read this session; the quotation below is therefore reused verbatim from that already-verified corpus entry rather than re-fetched, disclosed here rather than presented as an independent re-verification. This clause's statement that no comparable California statute overriding an equity plan's own forfeiture-on-termination terms was located rests on the plain text of section 227.3 (which names only vacation) together with a review of the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published glossary (letters E, S, and V, each fetched and byte-compared across two User-Agent headers this session), which contains no entry for equity compensation, stock options, RSUs, restricted stock, or vesting; that same review also did not surface any California statute requiring an employer to disclose equity status or exercise deadlines specifically at termination, a gap disclosed here rather than an invented requirement. Neither review is an exhaustive canvass of the entire Labor Code, and CourtListener's unavailability this session means no case law search for a judicially created exception was possible; this clause reports what was and was not found this session rather than asserting the absence is definitive. This is one state's law; it does not address whether any other state has enacted a broader statute reaching equity compensation specifically.

FEDERAL TAX LAW'S POST-TERMINATION EXERCISE WINDOW FOR INCENTIVE STOCK OPTIONS
Federal tax law's favorable treatment for an incentive stock option ("ISO") — deferring taxation until the underlying stock is later sold, rather than at exercise — is conditioned on the option holder having remained an employee of the granting corporation, or a qualifying parent, subsidiary, or successor corporation, continuously up until a point no earlier than three months before the option is exercised. Once employment ends, an ISO exercised more than three months later no longer meets this condition, and the exercise is treated under federal tax law as an exercise of a nonstatutory stock option rather than an ISO for tax purposes. This three-month figure is a federal tax-qualification condition on favorable ISO tax treatment, not itself a statutory deadline after which the option is forfeited; whether the option agreement or equity plan sets its own, separate post-termination exercise deadline — after which the option lapses entirely, regardless of its tax treatment — is a matter of that agreement's own terms, described in this document as: 90 days from the termination date. A post-termination exercise window commonly used in practice and often described as roughly ninety days is, on this statute's own text, an approximation of the three-month period this federal tax rule specifies for retaining ISO tax treatment, not a period this or any statute itself requires an option to remain exercisable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "at all times during the period beginning on the date of the granting of the option and ending on the day 3 months before the date of such exercise, such individual was an employee of either the corporation granting such option, a parent or subsidiary corporation of such corporation, or a corporation or a parent or subsidiary corporation of such corporation issuing or assuming a stock option in a transaction to which section 424(a) applies."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 422(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, employment-status condition for incentive stock option tax treatment (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/422)
  Known gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 422(a)(2)), not California state law, and it applies the same way regardless of which state's law otherwise governs the employment relationship. This clause cites a single statutory subsection; the surrounding provisions of the same section — defining what counts as an "incentive stock option" in the first place (§ 422(b)), and separately extending the three-month period to one year for a person disabled within the meaning of a cross-referenced statute (§ 422(c)(6)) — are not quoted or independently addressed here, since they define eligibility and a specific disability exception this clause does not resolve. The statutory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause does not address nonqualified stock options (which carry no comparable federal statutory holding-period or post-termination timing condition), restricted stock units (which are generally taxed on vesting rather than exercise and so raise no comparable exercise-window question), or the separate, contract-based question of what post-termination exercise deadline any specific option agreement or equity plan actually sets — that deadline is a matter of the specific agreement's own terms, not this statute. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

STATEMENT OF EQUITY COMPENSATION STATUS AT TERMINATION
Jordan Lee identifies the following equity compensation granted by Acme, Inc. as outstanding as of October 1, 2026:

Type of equity award(s): incentive stock options

Equity plan or option agreement under which granted: 2020 Equity Incentive Plan

Vesting status as of October 1, 2026 (vested and unexercised, unvested and forfeited, partially vested, or other — as determined by the terms of the equity plan or option agreement, not by this document): 10,000 shares vested; 5,000 shares unvested and forfeited

Post-termination exercise window stated in the applicable equity plan or option agreement, if any: 90 days from the termination date

This statement records Jordan Lee's current understanding of these facts. It is not a determination by any court, plan administrator, or other body of what portion of this equity is actually vested, exercisable, or owed, and it does not modify the terms of the equity plan or option agreement under which the equity was granted.
